blockMcqs.question: What core trade-off does an index make?
options: Faster writes, slower reads
Faster reads, slower writes and more space
Less disk space, slower reads
Faster reads with no downsides
blockMcqs.explanation: An index speeds reads by providing a lookup structure, but every write must update it and it consumes extra disk space.

blockMcqs.question: Why can a table have only one clustering index?
options: SQL syntax only allows one CREATE INDEX
The file can have only one physical row order
Clustering indexes require a primary key
Secondary indexes are always clustered
blockMcqs.explanation: A clustering index defines the physical storage order of rows on disk; only one physical order is possible per file.

blockMcqs.question: Which index type has one entry per disk block, not per record?
options: Dense index
Secondary index
Bitmap index
Sparse index
blockMcqs.explanation: A sparse index has one entry per block and only works when records are sorted by the key, using much less space than a dense index.

blockMcqs.question: What key structural feature makes B+ trees ideal for range queries?
options: Internal nodes store all data pointers
The tree is always exactly 3 levels deep
Leaf nodes are linked in a sorted chain
Each node holds exactly two children
blockMcqs.explanation: B+ tree leaf nodes are linked sequentially, so a range scan traverses to the start key then follows the chain — no backtracking through the tree.

blockMcqs.question: What problem does dynamic hashing solve that static hashing cannot?
options: Range queries across multiple buckets
Bucket overflow when data volume changes
Sorting results in hash order
Using less CPU than B+ trees
blockMcqs.explanation: Static hashing fixes the bucket count, so growing data causes overflow chains. Dynamic hashing grows the bucket directory as data grows, keeping lookup efficient.

blockMcqs.question: Bitmap indexes work best on columns with how many distinct values?
options: Millions of distinct values
Exactly one distinct value
A few distinct values (low cardinality)
More distinct values than rows
blockMcqs.explanation: Low-cardinality columns (e.g., gender, status) produce compact bitmaps. High-cardinality columns produce one huge bitmap per value, wasting space.

blockMcqs.question: What makes an index 'covering' for a given query?
options: It covers the entire table with one index entry
It includes every column the query needs to read
It is built on the primary key column
It uses a bitmap for each column
blockMcqs.explanation: A covering index satisfies the query entirely from the index structure, so the engine never needs to go back to the main table (no heap fetch).

blockMcqs.question: Which scenario shows an index making performance WORSE?
options: Range scan on a date column with millions of rows
Point lookup on a unique email column
INSERT-heavy OLTP table with many indexes
Query on the primary key of a large table
blockMcqs.explanation: Every INSERT must update all indexes on the table. A write-heavy table burdened with many indexes pays constant overhead, making writes slower than without them.
